analysis.one_liner: Hands fracking regulation entirely to the states, stripping federal oversight even on federal land.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: introduced March 29, 2012, it was referred to four committees and died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would give each state the only power to regulate hydraulic fracturing — fracking — for oil, gas, and geothermal drilling, and would put fracking on federal land under state law instead of federal law [S2][S3]. That would stop the Interior Department's plan, announced in 2011, to write federal fracking rules for drilling on public land and national forests [S3]. The bill never advanced past its initial committee referrals, and it expired when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013 [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain the most. They would deal with a single regulator in each state rather than both state agencies and federal agencies, would avoid any federal fracking rule for drilling on public land, and would face no national baseline for well standards — only whatever each state chooses to require [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Grants each state sole authority to write and enforce every fracking rule, permit, and guidance within its borders, removing any federal role [S2][S3].

Puts fracking on federal land — public lands, national forests, Bureau of Reclamation land, and Corps of Engineers land — under the law of whichever state the land sits in, rather than federal law [S3].

The bill's own findings note that the Interior Secretary announced in 2011 an intent to issue new federal fracking rules for federal land; this bill would prevent any such rule from taking effect [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People who live near fracking operations would bear the risk: their drinking water and air would be protected only by their own state's rules, which vary widely in rigor, with no federal floor [S2][S3]. Because federal land belongs to all Americans, national forests and public lands could be fracked under only the host state's standards, which may not reflect the interests of the people who own that land [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Residents near fracking wells and public lands

drawbacks.text: By making state law the only authority, the bill would leave no federal backstop for drinking water near fracking wells, and states' oil and gas rules differ greatly in stringency, so protections would depend entirely on where a person lives [S2][S3].

Fracking on national forests and other federal land would be governed solely by the host state's law, even though that land is held in trust for the whole country, not just that state's residents [S3].

The bill cites older studies finding no confirmed fracking contamination of drinking water, but it would lock in that conclusion as law just as federal agencies were beginning to write updated rules for drilling on federal land, foreclosing stricter national standards [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The industry case is that overlapping state and federal permitting slows drilling, and states already regulate oil and gas operations [S3]. But the cost falls on people with no say in another state's rules: a single national forest or public aquifer could be fracked under the weakest applicable state standard, and the bill was written precisely to block the federal fracking rules then being developed for federal land [S3]. The savings to drillers come directly out of the uniform, national level of protection the bill would remove.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees and five subcommittees, none of which took it up, and it expired when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013 without a hearing or a vote [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Louie Gohmert introduced the bill on March 29, 2012, joined by 38 Republican cosponsors and no Democrats [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Natural Resources, Agriculture, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Energy and Commerce committees on the day it was introduced [S5].
Within the following weeks it was split among five subcommittees, including Environment and the Economy, Water Resources and Environment, and Energy and Mineral Resources [S5].
No committee, subcommittee, or chamber ever took further action on it, and the bill died at the end of the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public kept the existing arrangement in which federal agencies retain authority over fracking on federal land, and the oil and gas industry did not get the exemption it sought. No one gained materially from the bill dying; the status quo simply continued.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal oversight survived; drillers gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: All 38 cosponsors were Republicans and the sponsor was a Republican; no Democrat signed on and no vote was ever taken [S4].

industries.note: The bill would remove federal fracking oversight, including the Interior Department's planned rules for drilling on federal land, leaving drillers answerable only to state regulators of their choosing's state. That saves companies permitting costs and compliance burdens while shifting the environmental and drinking-water risk onto nearby residents [S2][S3].

The bill would make each state the permanent, sole regulator of fracking within its borders, locking in the state permitting system that the bill's own findings praise. States would gain authority, but the public would lose the federal baseline some states' rules do not provide [S2][S3].
The bill covers geothermal as well as oil and gas production, so geothermal drillers would also be freed from any federal fracking requirements. The effect is small relative to oil and gas [S2][S3].
